title: The Real Bottleneck in Explicit Instruction The Teachers Working Memory
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: SoL in the Wild argues that explicit instruction effectiveness depends critically on the teachers working memory, not just students. The author outlines how teachers manage simultaneous cognitive demands during instruction—explaining content, monitoring understanding, asking questions, managing behavior, and pacing—and how cognitive overload degrades instructional quality. Rather than constantly making decisions in real time, effective teachers proactively offload thinking into advance planning, building routines and procedures that protect the mental resources instruction depends on.
points: Teachers experience real-time cognitive load as complex as that facing students, managing simultaneous demands of explanation, monitoring, questioning, behavior management, and pacing decisions.

When teacher working memory is overloaded, instruction degrades in measurable ways: explanations become rambling, checks for understanding are sporadic, pacing suffers, and teaching becomes reactive rather than proactive.

The most powerful teaching moves—offloading, proceduralization, and building routines—work not primarily for organization but to protect teacher working memory and enable clearer, more responsive instruction.
quotes: We frequently talk about students' working memory as if it's the central bottleneck in learning. And it is. But there's a critical piece not discussed enough: What about the teacher's working memory?
The effectiveness of my explicit instruction isn't just about what I know or plan, but what I can manage in real time.

Highly effective teachers aren't just knowledgeable about how we learn and how to teach based on that evidence. They're excellent at proactively protecting their own working memory just as much as they do their students.
Offloading is the deliberate act of moving thinking out of the moment of instruction and into planning. Instead of making constant decisions in real time, those decisions are made in advance.

If a teacher's working memory is overloaded with extraneous information and decisions, explicit instruction can rapidly turn into rambling explanations, missed opportunities to check for understanding, poor pacing, and reactive instead of proactive teaching.” Archived from SoL in the Wild on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
